title: Classical Versification Metrics (Al-ʿArūḍ)
source: Original instructional lesson authored for this application (syllabus ref: Haywood & Nahmad Ch. 52; Ryding Appendix II)
objectives: Understand the prosodic system of al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad based on short/long syllable patterns.
Distinguish prosodic units: cord (sabab) and peg (watad).
Recognize the names and rhythms of major classical meters (الطَّوِيلُ, الكَامِلُ, البَسِيطُ, الوَافِرُ) and rhyme (al-qāfiyah).

sections.heading: The Metrical System of Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad
sections.body: Classical Arabic poetry is quantitative—built on alternating patterns of short (vowelled consonant, ᴗ) and long (vowelled + vowelless/long vowel, —) syllables grouped into mnemonic feet (tafʿīlāt) derived from ف-ع-ل. Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad systematized sixteen classical meters (buḥūr).

sections.label: Prosodic Writing (Al-Kitābah al-ʿArūḍiyyah)
sections.summary: In scansion, write ONLY what is pronounced: double every shaddah into two consonants (CْCَ), write tanwīn as a vowelless nūn (نْ), and drop silent letters (such as hamzat al-waṣl mid-line).

sections.translation: Mnemonic scansion pattern of one hemistich of al-Ṭawīl.
sections.notes: Each classical verse (bayt) consists of two equal hemistichs (ṣadr and ʿajuz) sharing the same meter and ending in a unified rhyme consonant (rawī).

sections.heading: Poetic License (Ḍarūrah)
sections.body: In classical verse, short final vowels at the end of a hemistich are lengthened for rhyme (ishbāʿ), and occasionally diptotes take tanwīn.
